speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In recent years, we have not only seen an increasing number of cyberattacks worldwide, but also a wider range of targets, including individuals, large organisations like Equifax, and Government agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Singapore remains an attractive target to attackers because of our high dependence on Internet-based transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In 2017 alone, we saw attacks against our Government agencies, universities, financial institutions, both large and small enterprises, and individuals who had their computers locked by ransomware.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Protection against cyberattacks needs to start with organisations and individuals taking responsibility for the cybersecurity of their own computer systems.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: However, it is also important for us to work collectively, especially in protecting our essential services, against cyberattacks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Computer systems directly involved in the provision of essential services are termed Critical Information Infrastructure (CII).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Even with efforts to protect CII, we cannot expect to detect and foil every cyberattack.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: This is why it is also necessary to investigate cybersecurity threats and incidents, and to mitigate the consequences of successful attacks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Currently, section 15A of the Computer Misuse and Cybersecurity Act (CMCA) empowers the Minister for Home Affairs to issue a certificate to authorise or direct a person or an entity to take measures to comply with requirements necessary to prevent, detect or counter a threat to any class of computers or computer services, if the Minister is satisfied that it is necessary to do so for the purpose of preventing, detecting or countering any threat to the national security, essential services, defence or foreign relations of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Parts 3 and 4 of the Bill set out a framework for CSA to request for cybersecurity information on CII and during investigations of cybersecurity threats and incidents.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Bill protects such information by requiring specified persons who obtain it when performing their functions or discharging their duties to keep it confidential, and by specifying the circumstances where it can be disclosed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Cybersecurity Bill does not provide powers to prosecute cybercriminals.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: CMCA and other relevant legislation will continue to govern the investigation and the prosecution of cybercrime perpetrators and the detection and apprehension of such offenders.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Bill is intended to apply concurrently with other laws and regulations enacted in Singapore, including existing sectoral laws.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In formulating this Bill, the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) and CSA studied cybersecurity legislation which other countries, such as Germany, Estonia, the United States (US), Thailand and Vietnam, have implemented or are considering.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: These laws cover areas, such as imposing obligations on CII owners to protect their CII, requiring cybersecurity audits to be conducted, making the reporting of cybersecurity incidents mandatory, encouraging companies to share cybersecurity information with the Government, prevention of cybersecurity attacks and, finally, industry regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Our Bill is in line with these international developments.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We also consulted industry associations, cybersecurity professionals, sector regulators, potential key CII stakeholders and the general public.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In response to requests for more time to provide feedback, we extended our public consultation to six weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: They shared the Government’s concerns on cybersecurity threats and the impact of cyberattacks on Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Respondents also provided useful feedback that allowed us to identify aspects of the Bill that could be refined when drafting the Bill, including simplifying the licensing framework.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clause 4 of the Bill allows the Minister-in-charge of Cybersecurity to appoint a Commissioner of Cybersecurity to administer the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: This appointment will be held by the Chief Executive of CSA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Today, CSA works with sector regulators to coordinate cybersecurity efforts to protect CII within their respective sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The sectors have varying levels of cybersecurity readiness, and sector regulators have varying legislative powers to regulate CII within their sectors on cybersecurity matters.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clause 4 allows the Minister to appoint Assistant Commissioners (ACs) to assist the Commissioner to oversee and enforce cybersecurity requirements on the CII owners.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The intention is to appoint senior officers from sector regulators as ACs to perform this role in respect of CII in their respective sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: This is because such officers understand the unique contexts and complexities of their sectors and will be best placed to advise the Commissioner on the necessary requirements so as to strike a balance between their sectors’ operational needs and national cybersecurity considerations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clause 7 allows the Commissioner to designate as a CII, any computer or computer system that is necessary for the continuous delivery of an essential service set out in the First Schedule, and the loss or compromise of the computer or computer systems will have a debilitating effect on the availability of the essential service.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: This clause also requires the Commissioner to inform the CII owner how he can submit representations against the designation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: CSA has worked closely with sector regulators to identify the list of essential services as set out in the First Schedule.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: An essential service is defined in clause 2 as any service essential to the national security, defence, foreign relations, economy, public health, public safety or public order of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: New essential services may be added from time to time to the First Schedule by the Minister exercising powers under the Bill if necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Bill will require CII owners to comply with statutory obligations to ensure the cybersecurity of their CII.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: No action under the Bill will be taken against CII owners for cybersecurity breaches so long as they comply with their obligations thereunder.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Non-compliance with CII-related obligations under Part 3 of the Bill will be an offence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: CII owners who disagree with particular decisions of the Commissioner, such as the CII designation, may appeal to the Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: To strengthen CSA’s ability to prevent and respond effectively to cybersecurity threats and incidents, Part 4 of the Bill empowers the Commissioner to investigate cybersecurity threats and incidents.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: These powers in clauses 19 and 20 are calibrated according to the severity of the cybersecurity threat or incident and measures required for response.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Commissioner may authorise incident response officers to exercise these investigation powers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In addition, the Minister has powers to require cybersecurity measures under clause 23 for the purpose of countering serious and imminent threats.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It is not our intent to use these powers to respond to each and every cybersecurity threat or incident in Singapore, as computer owners are ultimately responsible for the cybersecurity of their own computers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clause 19 allows the Commissioner to request persons to furnish specified information that is necessary for the investigation of cybersecurity threats or incidents, for the purpose of: (a) assessing their impact or potential impact; (b) preventing any or further harm arising from the same cybersecurity incident; and (c) preventing a further cybersecurity incident.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The maximum penalty under clause 19 is $5,000 or six months’ imprisonment or both, for offences, such as willfully misstating information or refusing to provide required information without reasonable excuse.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clause 20 allows the Commissioner to authorise incident response officers to exercise more intrusive investigative powers as are necessary to investigate and prevent serious cybersecurity threats or incidents.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: For example, the Commissioner may require the owner of a computer to scan the computer for cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clause 20(3) prescribes a set of criteria for determining what constitutes a "serious" cybersecurity threat or incident, such as when it creates a risk of significant harm being caused to a CII.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Such powers are necessary given the potential impact from serious cybersecurity threats and incidents, which can disrupt our essential services, potentially cause physical damage and harm, and affect our economy and our way of life.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Bill clearly spells out how these powers may be exercised.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: These powers are calibrated and there are safeguards built into the Bill, such as what I have just described.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clause 23 allows the Minister to authorise or direct any person or organisation to take measures for the purpose of countering serious and imminent threats.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clause 23 is a re-enactment with slight modifications of section 15A of CMCA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: CMCA will correspondingly be renamed as the Computer Misuse Act, or CMA in short, at the same time that the Cybersecurity Bill is passed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The offences and penalties under clause 23 are the same as those under section 15A of CMCA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Bill recognises that information disclosed to CSA under the Bill is often confidential.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Information disclosed to CSA may be used to determine if a computer system is a CII (clause 8), technical information relating to a CII (clause 10), or information given pursuant to an investigation into a cybersecurity threat or incident (clause 19 or 20).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Therefore, under clause 43, the Commissioner and other specified persons must preserve the secrecy of information that may come to their knowledge as a result of performing their functions or discharging their duties under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Such information includes matters relating to a computer system, as well as the identity of persons who furnished the information.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It will be a criminal offence under clause 43(4) if specified persons fail to preserve the secrecy of such information or unlawfully discloses such information.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The maximum penalty is $10,000, or one year’s imprisonment, or both.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: However, clause 43 provides for the sharing of information in certain circumstances, such as for the purposes of prosecution under the Bill, or to disclose to the Police any information which discloses the commission of an offence under CMA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We recognise other persons may have information on whether CII owners are complying with their obligations specified in Part 3 of the Bill, and we want to encourage the disclosure of such information to the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clause 45 provides for the protection of these informers in relation to proceedings for an offence under Part 3 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: As cybersecurity risks become more widespread, the demand for credible cybersecurity services will grow.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Some cybersecurity services can be sensitive because the service providers performing them can have significant access into their clients’ computer systems and networks and gain a deep understanding of the cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Such services, if abused, can compromise and disrupt the clients’ operations even after the service provider’s job has been completed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Furthermore, there is asymmetry of information; many organisations, especially smaller ones, may not know which cybersecurity service providers are ethical or offer reliable services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Part 5 of the Bill provides for a licensing framework for cybersecurity service providers that service the Singapore market.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: For a start, the licensing framework will be a light touch in view that this is a new initiative and there is a need to strike a good balance between industry development and cybersecurity needs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: These providers have access to sensitive information from their clients, and the services are also relatively mainstream in our market and, hence, have a significant impact on the overall cybersecurity landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clause 24 requires providers of licensable cybersecurity services that are specified in the Second Schedule to apply for a licence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It will be an offence to provide such services without a licence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We do not intend to require companies to be licensed for providing licensable cybersecurity services to their related companies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In addition, the term "cybersecurity service", as defined in clause 2, only covers a service provided by a person for a reward to another person, and excludes a service provided in-house to an employer.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Financial penalties may be imposed under clause 32 for non-compliance with licensing conditions or for other regulatory breaches that are not an offence, such as the failure to keep and retain proper records.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The maximum penalty is $10,000 for each non-compliance but not exceeding, in the aggregate, $50,000.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The licensing officer is required under clause 33 to give licensees an opportunity to submit representations before the imposition of financial penalties.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We will partner public and private sector stakeholders in the journey to strengthen the protection of CII.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: CSA will also implement programmes to help the sector regulators assist CII owners in getting ready to fulfil their obligations under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We will also engage the industry further on the licensing conditions for licensed cybersecurity service providers under clause 27 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I work for a firm that provides cybersecurity and risk services.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have seen growing evidence of how countries are being threatened by digital sabotage which targets essential services to cause disruption to the economy, as well as to confuse and demoralise citizens.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Ukraine experience, as the Minister has shared earlier on, was one that is almost becoming a cyber-hacking "testbed" for other foreign state actors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nearly a year later, on 17 December 2016, a single transmission substation in northern Kiev lost power.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These instances of sabotage took place on the tail of a political revolution in Kiev and the annexation of Crimea.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have been fortunate that the recent Wannacry, Meltdown and Spectre malware attacks have not disrupted our essential services.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nonetheless, these attacks are a clear and present danger to a compact nation like Singapore, where a politically or militarily motivated actor can use cyber warfare to sabotage our critical infrastructure and economy.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Current international laws have not been effective to address cross-border hacking and state-sponsored attacks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In most cases, agencies have had difficulty to pin down hacking incidents to individuals or governments.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe the Cybersecurity Bill is a good start for Singapore to ensure that our essential services and sectors are well-protected and defended to prevent criminals or state players from threatening our economy and our way of life.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome that this Bill looks into proactive measures to have owners of CIIs to be more accountable for reporting and the security readiness of their CIIs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important that relevant stake players provide timely reports of attacks and I fully support that the CSA drive industry-wide knowledge sharing and push for effective cyber defence measures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Countries, such as Germany, Japan and the US, have already enacted cybersecurity legislation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Thailand and Vietnam are also considering similar legislation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, this Bill is a timely reflection of our commitment to securing our nation and our status as a top-tier international hub and financial hub.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: From the view of the industry, one of the key concerns will be whether the cost of compliance and the costs of systems upgrades will be significant.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Consumers will also be concerned if these additional costs will be passed on to them, as many of these CII owners provide essential services, such as transport, water, electricity and communications.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must strike a balance to protect our national and citizens' interests but yet be clear on what security standards and architectures that CIIs need to comply with, so that the costs incurred in upgrades and security operations will not overburden industry and consumers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The cyber arms race is not about to recede and will only intensify and hackers will continue to try to find weaknesses in systems to exploit.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, I would like to make some suggestions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One, it will be ideal if CSA can take the lead, together with the sector regulators, to set industry-wide leading practices, shared services and threat intelligence, so that CII players can achieve security readiness in a cost-efficient manner and yet be effective in deterring and responding to security threats.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Two, this Bill will drive greater accountability from the CII owners, and failure to comply with this new law will be criminal in nature.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support the need to make the owners of the CIIs accountable, but I hope that CSA be very clear on the benchmarks or, if appropriate, security architectures that CII owners need to comply with upfront.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will also help the relevant CIIs to plan their security roadmap effectively and better understand the investments they need to make.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, the industry risks putting in piecemeal measures that could be costly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It would also not be good if CII owners take a reactive approach to only wait for audit results and taking action only when told that they need to comply to them from time to time.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Under the law, they will only be criminally penalised when they have not complied with a directive from the Commissioner.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Three, I would like also to suggest that the Ministry and the sector regulators consider funding R&D for cybersecurity technology and operations centrally or within sectors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The involvement of CSA and sector regulators can catalyse CII operators to share findings and insights to accelerate cybersecurity enhancements.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are many common insights that could be derived from research and leading practices within specific sectors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will help CII operators develop quicker and more effectively.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is the timeline that CIIs have come back that they need to get fully ready and compliant?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Citizens will be concerned that, as part of investigations, the authorities may need to access data residing within the CIIs and this may breach the privacy of individuals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the safeguards put in place to ensure that the broad investigation powers under this Bill do not invade the privacy of individuals and consumers?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is the rationale of keeping the Acts separate as they both deal with essentially cybercrime?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How would enforcement operations be divided across the two pieces of legislation to deal with cybercriminals involved in attacks, such as Ransomware, Malware or Distributed Denial of Services (DDOS) attacks?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The same crime can technically be applied across both critical infrastructure and non-critical, and common information technology (IT) systems.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, is there a duplication of effort or duplication of resources?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What features under the new Bill will enable our agencies to better address as well crimes arising from overseas actors?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given that some CII operators may use technologies, such as cloud services or outsourced managed services based overseas, how does the regulator plan to designate these systems as CII, as the data and application may not reside, wholly or in part, in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support this initiative as it will put in place a credible ecosystem to support our CIIs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this emerging field of cybersecurity, there are many global experts, or even white-hat hackers, whose expertise may be useful as freelancers to advise CII owners.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why does the Ministry not consider allowing individuals to be contracted by the CII owners?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: From a manpower perspective, Mr Speaker, cybersecurity resources are in demand today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How is the Ministry planning to uplift the capabilities that we have to fulfil demand once the Bill comes into force?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Do we have a significant capability gap today and how long does the Ministry estimate for us to fulfil this gap?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Ministry may also wish to facilitate manpower exchanges with leading technology research labs or CIIs overseas with leading practices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of the CIIs named are in sectors that are facing slowdown and may find it difficult to prioritise funds for this in the short term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such a capability fund can help adoption, especially within the immediate future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Countries have the ability to combine conventional and cyber tactics to weaken an opponent's defence by disrupting its essential services and its economy, and also to maximise confusion and uncertainty using both simple and sophisticated technologies in innovative ways.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is timely to stress the importance of strengthening our CIIs in the interest of national security.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have been developing our Total Defence capabilities across five pillars – military, civil, economic, social and psychological defence.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It has worked for us for several decades.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this digital era and considering the emerging threat of hybrid warfare, it may be time for the Government to update our approach.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Its ambit and reach are understandably wide in view of the reliance both the public and private sectors, including individuals, place on computer programmes, systems and services, and the devastating prospect of debilitating cyberattacks on critical sectors of the economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For that reason, my clarifications will be limited to the Bill's broad principles and impulse, centring on queries that pertain to the operation of the envisaged Cybersecurity Act in practice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first clarification pertains to clause 7 of the Bill covering companies and entities that host CII that are partly located overseas for business reasons or simply logistical convenience.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a part of a Singaporean entity's CII ecosystem may be located overseas, how does the Bill ensure that this bifurcation does not render a particular CII susceptible to compromise or cyberattacks since CII computers and computer systems based overseas are not covered by this Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, in light of the feedback received, how common are such hybrid arrangements amongst public and private sector CII owners and is the Ministry concerned that some entities may seek to locate some elements of their CII overseas to hedge against the reach of the Act and, as a consequence, compromise its regulatory reach?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have a similar clarification with regard to ownership of a CII, particularly if the owner is an offshore entity or individual.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What regulatory oversight will the Bill realistically have over CII owners who operate outside our jurisdiction, and would this not represent a loophole?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Feedback on such costs were received by the Ministry and there was a suggestion that grants should be extended to help organisations offset these costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, I understand from feedback to the Ministry that there was some concern about what constituted a significant security incident.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The language of the Bill in clause 14 focuses on prescribed incidents suggesting that subsidiary legislation will clarify such words and terms.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the Bill imposes a duty on owners of CII to report incidents, can the Minister give the House a general sense, with examples of the specific thresholds of hypothetical incidents which may require reporting under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How far does this Bill go to take a CII owner to task for non-reporting should a similar Uber-like episode occur after this Bill becomes law?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What other actions would the Government consider against entities that are negligent in securing their computer systems, particularly if such an incident is aggravated through willful concealment?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, clause 19 of the Bill gives extraordinarily broad powers to the Commissioner of Cybersecurity and his officers to investigate cybersecurity threats and incidents against companies, entities and even individuals with respect to any computer or computer system in Singapore, not just CIIs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The ambit of these powers is best exemplified by clause 19(1)(a) of the Bill, which gives the Commissioner and any authorised officer the power to remove or make copies of a hard disk, for example, even if it is only to assess the impact or potential impact of a cybersecurity threat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For avoidance of any doubt, notwithstanding the remarks in the Report on Public Consultation on the draft Cybersecurity Bill where it was stated that such powers are to be applied in a calibrated manner and, more importantly, in response to major cybersecurity incidents against non-CIIs, can the Minister confirm the envisaged threshold of what qualifies as a major incident, so that the House is reassured that the Commissioner's powers will be used very judiciously and not against Government critics and individuals?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to the Uber example, does the Government foresee using such powers against foreign companies that operate in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, I am concerned about how much Singaporeans are actually aware of their online signature and the importance of cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While we seek to protect key infrastructure against cyberattacks, every Singaporean, who uses his or her smartphone to pay for goods and services or uses it as a social engagement tool, is susceptible to cyberattack or hacking.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This prospect is likely to increase as Singapore undertakes its Smart Nation drive with more focus and coordination.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The year 2017 has been called the Year of the Data Breach.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: New malware samples reached an all-time high of 57.6 million in the third quarter of 2017, according to McAfee Labs Threat Report December 2017.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not just a matter of privacy or lost personal data – there are financial, security, proprietary interests at stake.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A class action suit was initiated in the US last year against Equifax for data breach.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They alleged that criminals used the stolen data to "apply for mortgages, credit cards, student loans, tap into bank debit accounts, file insurance claims and rack up substantial debts." Stolen identity also poses an international problem, a terrorist problem.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last month, Thai police arrested a man who allegedly forged passports, including Singapore passports, for groups, including a terrorist group.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, breaches in cybersecurity can have debilitating effects on essential services.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, what we are debating today is serious.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Wannacry was a ransomeware worm and, by "worm", we are talking about a malware programme that is able to self-replicate to infect other computers and infiltrate through the connections in a computer network.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The NotPetya in Ukraine, which utilised a hacked version of a major accounting programme widely used in Ukraine, affected companies in many different sectors, from shipping to pharmaceuticals and to outside Ukraine through multinational companies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Worse still, NotPetya encrypts files with no chance of recovery, that is, it was not a ransomeware.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Stuxnet, a different computer worm, caused a proportion of machinery in Iran’s nuclear facility to spin out of control in 2010.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This cyberattack was executed through infected Universal Serial Buses (USBs), overcoming the "air gap".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since then, new methods to jump over an air gap has emerged.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: No sector has been spared cyberattacks, with commercial and healthcare sectors targeted the most.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This threat is not something remote to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although Singapore’s critical infrastructure was not hit by Wannacry, Singapore malls were among the victims of that ransomware.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Within the past five years, there were notable occasions of security breaches.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2014, Singapore’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs' IT system was breached.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One thousand and five hundred SingPass users' IDs and passwords were reported to be potentially compromised and illegally accessed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, the National University of Singapore (NUS) and the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) reported an attack by "advanced persistent threat" (APT) actors that sought to "steal research and Government-related information." These and many other instances are like red, flashing lights warning us to be vigilant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I concur with Minister Yaacob Ibrahim's point that we need to act and we need to act now.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They could hit us faster than we can react and they could hit us harder than we can imagine.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, this forward-looking Bill goes upstream to secure our information infrastructure through preventive and reactive compliance, so as to give us the upper hand and arsenal we can deploy against those who seek to do us harm.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To facilitate accountability and promote compliance, clause 45 protects informers’ identities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In today's age of technology, more infrastructure is being built, not from concrete and steel but, rather, in the realm of intangible cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This trajectory is bound to continue as Singapore moves toward being a "Smart Nation".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some of the future initiatives announced recently include digitalising of healthcare records even at the level of a private general practitioner (GP) through the National Electronic Health Record (NEHR) and the promoting of cashless payments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we seek to increase leveraging the conveniences and prowess of modern technology, it is critical that we protect and prevent attacks and crises from threatening our cyber infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The important place they have in the running of our country is reflected in this Bill’s designation of CII.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This designation spans 11 broad areas of essential services set out in its First Schedule.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cybersecurity in a computer network would only be as strong as the weakest link.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A single vulnerability may be exploited to infect other areas and other computers in the network.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the Commissioner’s written directions may be issued to a class of CII owners under clause 12(1); the Commissioner to direct more frequent audit above the two years "in any particular case" under clause 15(1)(a).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Bill also provides for flexible codes of practice under clause 11 to be promulgated to promote best practices in cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important that this regulatory skeleton provides sufficient flexibility to accommodate for changes in the realm of cyberspace and allow for careful calibration of regulation in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If there are too many regulations, the higher threshold to entry may perhaps shrink our well of cybersecurity expertise to draw from, harming our cybersecurity resilience, for example, through an over-reliance on a single provider which may multiply knock-on effects of a breach.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, the regulatory framework, in my view, needs to remain flexible for future refinement of regulatory controls.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This flexibility is especially crucial because technology is an ever-evolving landscape.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cybersecurity depends on innovation to keep up, keep ahead and remain effective.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Recently, MINDEF invited white hat hackers to hack into MINDEF’s Internet-facing domains.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This method of exposing vulnerabilities maximised the talent pool available locally and overseas.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It places our country to better respond to, prevent and secure the integrity of our computer systems through a strong, yet flexible, regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For these reasons, Mr Speaker, I strongly support the Bill.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, indeed, a step in the right direction in light of more and more sophisticated cyber threats which have crippled a country's CII, such as that which happened to NHS in the UK, as the Minister has alluded to.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The terrible impact of the cyberattack devastated hospitals and GP clinics in the UK.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Its Cyber Security Centre was working round the clock to bring its systems back online when this attack resulted in surgeries being cancelled, ambulances being diverted and patient records missing after it became the highest-profile victim of a global ransomware attack and was faced with renewed concern about the strength of its infrastructure.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This malware blocks access to any files on PC until a ransom is paid.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This could have been a situation in Singapore if we are not better prepared.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The concern over cybersecurity becomes more imminent with the Ministry of Health’s (MOH's) direction to move into NEHR for patients, which is an excellent initiative.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With access to one patient record across public and private healthcare sectors, framework, structure, audits, cybersecurity governance and oversight, including educating the stakeholders and providing relevant continuous training, becomes paramount.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Our country’s information infrastructure has to be protected and well-preserved from infiltration and attack in the name of cyber-terrorism.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The importance of working with the various stakeholders cannot be over-emphasised and it is equally pertinent to ensure the relevant sectors work closely with one another to implement the intricacies of the Bill and to ensure the proposed requirements are adhered to.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I believe implementing it would be more challenging than enforcing the Bill.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Licensing cybersecurity service providers may not be a popular move but a necessary one to ensure that they meet the security needs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to propose the following suggestions for consideration.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There needs to be a structured means of briefing the companies, especially small and medium enterprises (SMEs), on guidelines to encourage them to adhere to the cybersecurity measures.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: They may also need borrowed expertise to put in place the secured means of protecting information as they serve as a third-party vendor to some clients.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It would be good for the Government to grow and provide a pipeline of those talents to assist these companies which will need them.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In the areas of training, the Government may consider grants to encourage individual personnel to take up cybersecurity courses or programmes to refresh their knowledge and to be updated on the latest advancements, as the industry transforms rapidly.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This can be tied to SkillsFuture cybersecurity upskilling grants.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: To enhance governance and oversight, it would be worthy to introduce an accredited framework for auditors to perform checks and provide guidance or advice on what companies can do to have a more secured portal.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Effective communication mechanism or efficient connectivity to promptly inform stakeholders and companies of the specific sector or sectors that could be potential target and how to take timely precaution will serve to act as preventive means.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Companies or individuals who proved to have unintentionally violated the requirements in the Bill, should be made to go through relevant cybersecurity programmes and this should be made compulsory.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, it would be useful to ensure that all staff of the industry be made to attend awareness programmes in this field, so as to better protect the critical information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The extensive commentary and feedback received during the public consultation for the Bill show that the public recognises the importance of cybersecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the responses to the feedback, we can also see the Government trying to balance the compliance burden on business with the necessary measures to protect the economy from cyberattacks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore’s cybersecurity strategy is a correct approach taken for a global city that depends on openness and connectedness to the world for its proper functioning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This approach can be described as a whole-of-Government approach that places public-private collaboration at the heart of the strategy with a strong future-oriented plan for capacity development and for value addition to the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill is an integral part of the strategy and expresses the strategy’s approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have three sets of clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first set is more general and has to do with the strategy and its implementation; the second, on the scope of the Bill; and the third, on the specific provisions of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was rather surprised that there is very little mention of MINDEF in the Paper.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was mentioned once in the Paper when it was noted that MINDEF formed part of the National Cyber Incident Response Teams with CSA, the Government Technology Agency (GovTech) and the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These teams are part of the plan to respond to Tier 1 cyber campaigns threatening national security and Tier 2 cyberattacks on a sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MINDEF is a 4G military force reliant on secure communications and information networks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should already have well-developed cybersecurity infrastructure and capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be a terrible waste if the military applications are not adapted for civilian use.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could the Minister share whether there are plans to synergise and share military cybersecurity knowledge and technology to develop and deepen our civilian cybersecurity infrastructure?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Afterall, as it is stated in the strategy Paper, cybersecurity is a way of putting Total Defence into action and everyone has a role in creating a safer cyberspace for everyone, and this must include the military.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are two other specific ways that the military could play a key role to realise our cybersecurity strategy objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are already observed in public commentary on the strategy and many have pointed to the Israeli military as a successful example.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, our military has a peculiar asset: the commitment of tens of thousands of full-time and operationally-ready National Servicemen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This represents a potentially significant investment of time, not only of manpower, but of brainpower, by our highly educated workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The time invested could be harnessed to serve both military and civilian cybersecurity needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A cybersecurity corps could be formed to train budding IT professionals when they are serving full-time National Service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deferment could also be considered for these young men to obtain degrees in cybersecurity first, so that they would hone their classroom skills in the military.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They could then enter the cybersecurity industry when they become operationally-ready and return to the military with enhanced knowledge and skills during their NSmen call-ups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a win-win method to develop a vibrant cybersecurity system for Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, our unique military institution could also be used to foster startups to develop Singapore’s cybersecurity industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is now well-known that the Israeli Defence Force acted as the incubator for the startups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have similar institutional features here, so there is no reason why the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) cannot also serve as such an incubator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be a win for the military and a win for our entrepreneurship sector and economy, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I move on now to the second set of clarifications on the scope of the Cybersecurity Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill defines "critical information infrastructure" in section 7 as the computer system "necessary for the continuous delivery of an essential service", the compromise of which would lead to a serious effect on the availability of the essential service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Essential service is defined in section 2 as "any service essential to national security, defence, foreign relations, economy, public health, public safety or public order of Singapore, and specified in the First Schedule".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am surprised that higher education and research institutions are not listed as essential service in the First Schedule and would like the Minister to clarify why this is so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are three reasons why I am surprised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appeared to be the work not of casual hackers but of carefully planned, sophisticated cyberattacks that might be aimed at stealing information related to the Government and research.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is an extreme cyberattack scenario which this Bill is aimed at defending against.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If our top public universities are being targeted by organised hackers, who could not be named by CSA for operational security reasons, and they were going after some precious information which, again, CSA could not reveal for security reasons, then there must be critical information residing in our universities and research institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, of course, a sophisticated, targeted cyberattack on our universities does not mean that the service provided by the universities is essential, as defined in the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am, however, inclined to argue that there is a lot of research that is going on in our universities and other associated research institutions that have to do with the continuous delivery of essential services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The theft of information related to these research projects could lead to cyberattacks or other forms of attack that could seriously affect the availability of essential services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, our universities are central to cybersecurity innovation and training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is in the vision that each of the six universities would become a "cybersecurity centre of excellence" developing its own area of specialisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The training of our cybersecurity workforce is also entrusted to the universities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What this means is that there is a lot of meta-information on cybersecurity residing in our universities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The theft of this meta-information could compromise the general resilience of our cybersecurity infrastructure or that of specific CIIs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I move on finally to the third and last set of clarifications that have to do with the duty to report cybersecurity incidents, as specified in section 14.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have two points of clarifications for this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is specific to section 14, and the second has to do with cybersecurity incident reporting in general.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is onerous because it enlarges the scope of regulation beyond the CII into a far larger field of secondary computer systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the owner of a CII, this would mean the requirement of detection mechanisms in secondary computer systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, section 14(2) is not clear whether it is a legal requirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister clarify whether it is a requirement for the owner of a CII to install detection mechanisms in secondary computer systems interconnected with the CII?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister also clarify whether this reporting requirement is, indeed, onerous, especially since MCI and CSA’s response to feedback during the consultation on the draft Bill stated that "computer systems in the supply chain supporting the operation of a CII will not be designated as CIIs", implying that the regulation would be more narrowly scoped.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, section 14(1)(b) is limiting, if the intention is to protect the CII from cyberattacks in adjacent interconnected computer systems, as the clause is now worded to limit regulation to only secondary computer systems under the owner’s control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What if the secondary computer system interconnected to the CII is not under the control of the CII owner?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does it mean that such a computer system would not pose a risk to the CII?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a secondary computer system not under the control of the CII would still pose a risk to the CII, then why limit reporting to secondary computer systems under the CII owner’s control?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the risk is the same regardless, then why not remove the need to report cybersecurity incidents in secondary computer systems altogether?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My final point has to do with the reporting of cybersecurity incidents beyond the CIIs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Threat reports issued by cybersecurity firms often point to the problem of under-reporting, as many companies and organisations often choose not to report or to reveal the full extent of cyberattacks and data thefts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is understandable, as sensational news reports of major data breaches would undermine trust in these organisations and affect the bottom line of businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, it is not viable for these organisations to hide such incidents from view, as it would erode the general resilience of cybersecurity infrastructure in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Afterall, large-scale organised cyberattacks would likely begin with trial runs of mini attacks on non-critical computer systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is an expression of our Total Defence culture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As such, I believe there is a greater role to be played by MINDEF to develop our cybersecurity capabilities and enhance our cybersecurity enterprises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also believe that the Government should look more closely at our Institutions of Higher Learning (IHLs) as they have already come under a severe cyberattack and their computer systems contain crucial information related to our essential services and meta-information related to our cybersecurity infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It will enhance the oversight and protection of cybersecurity for our CII sectors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am heartened to note that we are building up our cybersecurity capabilities on a solid foundation and that the Government has been investing in developing a robust system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we can do better to raise our cybersecurity standard.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I agree with the Committee’s assessment that these lapses, which cut across agencies, are significant in view of the IT security threats today.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: PAC noted that the Ministry of Finance (MOF) has taken steps to deal with this problem on a whole-of-Government level, including the establishment of an interagency work group.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At least one of the lapses originated from an IT vendor, which had been warned.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, CSA noted that CII owners have the option to impose cybersecurity requirements contractually on their vendors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On one hand, I am concerned that this option may result in vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If CII owners choose not to impose cybersecurity requirements on their vendors, how robust will our systems be?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even if they do, will there be checks or audits to ensure our cybersecurity requirements are being met by the engaged vendors?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, vendors, some of which are SMEs, may find it difficult to cope with added costs, for example, third-party costs, should they be bound by contractual cybersecurity obligations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although reporting is compulsory, vendors, especially small ones, may not want to report as that means taking staff away from work to attend to investigations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Small companies are most vulnerable and their vulnerability may impact the CIIs which engaged them due to the sharing of data.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to be absolutely thorough to ensure that our systems are not being compromised through such weak links.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I now move on to the point on licensing of individual cybersecurity professionals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I am worried that, without licensing, we may be exposing ourselves to greater risks in the future.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How do we minimise such exposures and ensure accountability and traceability?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Similarly, for personnel responsible for cybersecurity, especially senior staff, do we have checks in place to ensure that we recruit suitable persons to make sure that they are of good character with adequate proper training and who upgrade their knowledge continuously?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The cybersecurity sector is evolving rapidly and we must be careful not to compromise Internet and system hygiene in our enthusiasm to support developments and innovations in this area.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While interconnectivity provides greater efficiency and productivity, in a way, we have also become more vulnerable and greater care must be taken across all networks.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has had its fair share of cybersecurity breaches these past few years.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have heard in this House about the attacks on MINDEF, as well as our two major universities, NUS and NTU.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While any cyberattack is of concern, to me, what is most worrying is that the attacks, the likes of those on the Singapore universities last year, were, as the authorities have depicted, carefully orchestrated and specifically targeted.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It was not the work of casual hackers.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But for how long? "We were just lucky", said Mr David Koh, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of CSA, to explain why Singapore escaped the brunt of global malware attacks like the WannaCry ransomware attack.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: According to Mr Koh, had these attackers targeted Singapore specifically, the consequences could have been quite disastrous.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This is why this Bill is so important.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In a world where nation-state actors are becoming bolder in their cross-border activities, we must ensure that our national security, including cyber defence, can withstand these cyberattacks by enemies we cannot see.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Cyber defence has to be a whole-of-country approach.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is the responsibility of every single person in this community, from the home owner to the business leader.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is one of Asia’s major technology hubs.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We are very highly connected and, as a result, very vulnerable to cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Our Smart Nation aspirations will bring many benefits but also many vulnerabilities if we are not vigilant and prepared.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In a recent newsletter, cyber technology company Apvera put Singapore at the top of the list of countries from which cyberattacks could be launched.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Just to clarify, this does not mean that Singaporeans are becoming hackers, but rather, we have become the No 1 potential launchpad for cybersecurity attacks because of our location, digitalisation, IT savviness as a people, and the increasing number of cloud-based and virtual servers.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the provisions of this Bill, Mr Speaker, public education has to be enhanced and ramped up.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, CSA commissioned a survey to find out about Singaporean attitudes to cybersecurity and cyber hygiene.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They store them on our computers and they write them down.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They also use the same passwords for multiple accounts, for work and personal accounts.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: More than six in 10 respondents connected to open, non-password protected wi-fi networks in public places.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Practices, such as these, pose a substantial risk to the security of their personal information and, ultimately, the cyber communities they are part of.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I would strongly encourage the Government to make these roadshows and campaigns a part of school curriculums right from the first time children use computers in schools.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Grassroots clubs and community centres should use this campaign to reach out to the elderly, too.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses should also play their part in bolstering their cybersecurity defence.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Too often, CEOs are happy to invest in IT systems only when it adds to their bottom line.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Few realise, until it is too late, that IT security will actually protect this bottom line.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Last month, in its review of the Auditor-General’s (AG's) Report for financial year (FY) 2016/2017, PAC cited recurring weaknesses in IT controls as a major weakness.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the lapses pointed out by PAC included: user accounts not being properly removed when required, and staff given access to accounts and data that they should not have access to.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What is alarming is that these weaknesses and lapses were pointed out in the past by the AG, and they were still recurring.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Though the Ministries concerned have made arrangements to ensure that such lapses do not happen again, this is yet another timely reminder that cybersecurity should not be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: All we need is just one lapse to bring down the entire system.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot take our security for granted and, in today’s digital world, cybersecurity is as important, if not more important, than military security, as the enemy is invisible and can strike anytime and anywhere.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are living in an increasingly interconnected world enabled by digital technology, and the inadvertent rise of Internet of Things (IoT) will accelerate our dependency on technology to an unprecedented level in the near future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore remains one of the most connected country in the world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The explosive growth of ICT has ushered in a golden age of digitalisation and has been instrumental in enabling research, applied science, healthcare, transportation and urban development, just to name a few areas.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Building upon a robust ICT infrastructure is also the vision of transforming Singapore into a Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, the exponential growth of ICT and our increasing dependency on digital systems have heightened our vulnerability to cyber incidents.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These cyber incidents can take the form of cybercrime aimed at siphoning money from corporations and individuals; cyber terrorism and espionage aimed at crippling Government systems and pilfering sensitive information; or even seemingly innocuous cyber pranks that could lead to widespread havoc and social disruption.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, our Government systems were also not spared from such incidents.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have heard various Members in the House already referring to the incidents and the attacks carried out against MINDEF and also our IHLs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I do, however, have some points that I would like to raise for discussion and consideration.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Clause 4 of the Bill has vested the Minister with the authority to appoint a Cybersecurity Commissioner and a team of high-ranking cybersecurity officials who have a wide range of duties pertaining to the cybersecurity efforts in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although the appointment of the team will help ensure that efforts across Ministries and Statutory Boards are coordinated and policies are implemented consistently, greater clarity perhaps needs to be given on how this jurisdiction will be established.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the recently established GovTech taking on the role of the Chief Information Officer (CIO) of the Government, and CSA already monitoring cybersecurity, how will the newly established centralised cybersecurity office work alongside these agencies?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we ensure that there is no duplication of duties and, more importantly, what is the unique value-add that the centralised cybersecurity office will bring to our cybersecurity ecosystem that GovTech and CSA are not already doing?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Bill has set out some guidelines regarding the criteria of designating CIIs, perhaps more consideration needs to be given also on how the status of a CII is designated and what constitutes the phrase, "essential services".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, clause 1 in Part 3 of the Bill suggests that a CII can be defined as a computer or computer system that is necessary for the continuous delivery of essential services in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although some services might not be regarded as "essential", they could be considered significant, and any disruption of these entities could have a serious socio-economic impact.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moreover, there could also be private organisations that would require the appropriate assistance, advice and, more critically, protection in this area, too.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On a related note, if an organisation’s computer system, especially a commercial or private one, is designated as a CII, how much access to its database would the cybersecurity office have?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, if the computer system contains sensitive personal data like health records from insurance companies or investment portfolios from private banks and private organisations, how would cybersecurity be balanced with the intrusion into the privacy of the individual?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I noted that the Minister earlier mentioned that cybersecurity officers are going to be bound by certain very clear guidelines and perhaps even legislation or laws with regard to ensuring confidentiality when they access such information.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I think we cannot deny that there are some potential ethical dilemmas that could arise when cybersecurity officers, in the course of their work, gain access to personal data that contains identifiers when the providers of that information did not give explicit consent for the information to be used or accessed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it might not fall strictly under the rubrics of the proposed Bill, how can we provisionally use the Bill to manage the issue of "fake news"?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am aware that the Parliamentary Select Committee will, no doubt, present its views on how the issue of fake news can be tackled in due time but, until then, can we utilise the provisions in this Bill to take action against the perpetrators of fake news?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If someone were to hack into a Government agency’s system and issue falsehoods via the agency’s website or automated broadcast system, then can the Government take issue with the perpetrators for committing a cybercrime and also prosecute them for what their hacking resulted in?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, there will always be deviant individuals who will use science and technology for criminal activities or subversive purposes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Consider how nuclear power has allowed humanity to make significant progress, yet that same nuclear power and capability, in the hands of the wrong individual, can have catastrophic consequences for humanity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Digitisation and Internet technological advancement are no different.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As much as they have tremendous benefits for humanity, there is a dark side to this as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At best, cyber pranksters can cause widespread inconvenience.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The Internet has undoubtedly been part of our life, be it at home, at work, or while we play.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
