text: We use the Internet directly or indirectly, so much so it is almost impossible to live without it – doing research for education, dynamic navigation while driving, exploring new recipes for the next party meal, or even searching for that box office movie.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The Internet is now becoming an indispensable part of our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Our high dependency on the Internet has made it a part of us.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Like many things which are a part of us, it can also be deemed to be private, until when it is violated.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This could mean loss of business, loss of self-esteem for an individual or even loss of life.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While we want to believe that the Internet is safe and secure, however, a dark side of it exists and must be managed and controlled.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It happened in April 2016, where my work computer was attacked by a software virus which eventually encrypted and locked all my data files.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This resulted in me not being able to open or run any of my files.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It was a complete disaster as all my work was stored in the computer.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It was also unfortunate that the virus attacked the backup files, both in my computer and the main server.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This eventually rendered me helpless as I could neither provide all the required information, nor could I prepare any information for my potential business acquisition.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I felt intruded and my personal space had been violated.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Mentally, I felt no difference than a person who had been physically violated.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I wished the authorities could have acted and the culprit be apprehended and be dealt with according to the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Eventually, I managed to recover all the attacked files through a third-party overseas service provider, but with a fee for a few thousand US dollars.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I felt that I was held ransom and the only way to recover all my files was to pay that ransom fee.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This is not right and should never happen at all.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, the truth is: it did not stop.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Not only did it not stop, in fact, more and bigger cyberattacks occurred in the preceding years.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that some of my colleagues had already shared this.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In October to December 2013, a cyberattack called "The Messiah" created havoc as several systems and portals were compromised.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Users were redirected to suspicious and unknown websites and this undermined the confidence of Internet users.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We always thought that our military should be the last place and institution for a cyberattack to occur.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This was considered as one of the major cyberattacks of the decade.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It spread through malicious emails with booby-trapped Microsoft (MS) Office document.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: From there, it downloaded and ran the installer and released the software virus and spread unknowingly.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This had a devastating effect as it attacked the purported highly secured Master Files which are the basis of the file structure system.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It was made with malicious intent with the objective to create havoc and misery to all parties, including individuals, agencies and institutions.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Such acts must never be condoned as it will only lead to unhappiness, anger and loss of faith.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I regard such acts as similar to any physical attack on a person, as the consequence from such attack is dire, if not even more.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: From mental anxieties for having felt violated in their personal space to loss of valuable data and information on one’s Internet-linked devices, such as a computer, mobile phone and others, becoming a victim of a cyberattack can lead to serious consequences.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, a regulatory framework over the owners of CIIs and cybersecurity service providers will provide an added boost in ensuring that Singapore has a robust cybersecurity framework overall.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is my hope that the regulatory framework be regularly reviewed with higher frequency and in tandem with the fast-changing Internet landscape.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I wholeheartedly support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Members of this House have talked about the possibilities, as well as the dangers, offered by the Internet and we talk a lot about cybersecurity threats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, I would not repeat those other than to point out the fact that Singapore is no less exposed to such threats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: On the contrary, as the financial services hub and a regional hub to many global corporations, we are among some of the most exposed countries in the world, making us an attractive proposition to hackers from around the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is key to see how vulnerable we are.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This stands to impact our reputation, credibility and position as a global corporate hub and a regional e-commerce platform.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For such an ambitious project, and to protect our business hub status, we need to make sure we have a strong cybersecurity framework and regime.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, I am very supportive of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, I would like to ask our Government to share more on an important issue which is: how do we keep watch on the guards?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, how about the companies we are entrusting to protect the cyber world here?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While we have certification regimes to manage such companies and ensure that they meet desirable quality standards, do we know enough about the people who are working in these companies?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Do these professionals, who are certified, have a vested interest in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And what if they have interests that are contradictory to Singapore's?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is certainly not a stretch of imagination that we have foreign interests among our cybersecurity professionals here who may leverage their positions in having access to secret and confidential platforms.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, re-examine the penalties for misuse of access to data, especially if the perpetrators are members of the cybersecurity industry who are supposed to guard the industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, cybersecurity could be promoted as an engine of growth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has emerged as a trusted business hub because of our trusted regulations, our strict regulations and because of our people's trusted reputation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Properly executed, Singapore could naturally become a premier trusted business hub for Asia and for the region with regard to cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government share our plans to grow and internationalise the industry?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government also share more about our manpower plans to prepare Singapore to take part in this exciting development?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But if we get this right, it can also create many opportunities for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I propose to take a 20-minute break now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.00 pm until 3.20 pm.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In 2016, the National Cyber Security Command (NCSC) saw cyberattacks of varying impacts across many sectors, including the defence, Government, banking and finance, and healthcare sectors.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The omnibus Cybersecurity Bill allows the Minister to appoint a Commissioner of Cybersecurity.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Commissioner is, in turn, empowered to designate a CII.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: There have been tweaks, Mr Speaker, since an early draft of this Bill was first released in July last year for consultation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I must disclose at this point that I was together with other scholars and students of the Singapore Management University, one of the respondents of this consultation exercise.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I am, therefore, pleased, Mr Speaker, with what has followed, with the refinements that have been made to this draft Bill and now the Bill before us.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, I am pleased in relation to the regime that now governs cybersecurity licensees.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond this, clause 19(6) also suggests and clarifies that a person is no longer obliged to produce to the incident response officer an email infected by a malicious programme or malware if that email contains information that is subject to legal professional privilege.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: A distinction is made between a non-disclosure agreement which would be a contractual document of privilege, but there is a distinction now being made with legal professional privilege.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, Mr Speaker, the Bill acknowledges that a compliance-driven approach to cybersecurity should not only be focused on a box-ticking exercise, of getting all the boxes ticked, but one that solves cybersecurity problems creatively and proactively, thereby instilling a risk-management culture.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Behind laws, Mr Speaker, it is this creative approach that will be our shield against cybersecurity threats and incidents; it is this risk-management culture that will see CII owners taking swift and appropriate measures to prevent, manage and respond to cybersecurity threats and incidents.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In this vein, permit me to pose a few further questions to the Minister.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Most importantly, or chief amongst them, I would say, are businesses that are involved in this sector.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What perhaps is the Ministry and CSA's plan to minimise additional compliance costs?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I know that compliance costs for audits, reporting and risk assessments can be exorbitant, and these costs are, unfortunately, likely to be passed down to the consumers, not to the owners themselves.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If these processes are not properly managed in Singapore, considerable sums could be unproductively spent.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to Part IV of the Bill which deals with responses to threats and incidents, can we have some examples of what might variously qualify as a “cybersecurity threat or incident of a severe nature” on the one hand, a “serious threat” on the other, and still on the third hand, which we do not have, an emergency level “serious and imminent threat”?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They are terms apart which I would say judges and lawyers would be very keenly looking at.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Can we have some guidance as to what this would be?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Third, will cloud services be impacted by this new regulatory framework?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill’s explanatory statement admits that the Commissioner’s wide-ranging powers of access to data in clause 20 is “intrusive”.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will this be seen as going against perhaps established data privacy and protection principles and potentially expose the data of the cloud service provider’s clients?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly so in a public cloud environment.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Bill have a chilling effect on the adoption of cloud services in Singapore, as cloud customers in both Singapore and elsewhere become increasingly concerned about the level of Government access to private data and perhaps may withdraw from such cloud services in time to come, even though these cloud services arguably claim to provide better cybersecurity than what we have beyond the cloud services?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This would be a pity as the cloud could enable new innovations, such as artificial intelligence (AI) and big data analytics, which will likely become the basis of future developments in technology and that, by all accounts, the Smart Nation and Digital Government Office wishes to support.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that codes of practice and standards of performance will provide more guidance to the relevant businesses on the actions that they must take to comply with the Bill.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Are there plans to adopt the best practices, specifically from the US and the UK in this regard?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I note that the US has a Cybersecurity Disclosure Act of 2015, which adopts a "comply or explain" procedure in certain circumstances.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will we be following that route or studying it at least?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I fear when I read that MINDEF, quite rightly, is looking at how even fitness trackers could become a portal for CII threat or incident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the proliferation of Internet devices and the growing scale of worldwide cyberattacks, such as the widespread WannaCry ransomware attack in 2017, the proposed provisions in this Bill are a much-needed step towards safeguarding our cyberspace and everyday security.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Considering the multifaceted cybersecurity threats that we face today, the Bill is encouraging in both breadth and depth.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is no doubt that cybersecurity is important for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our highly interconnected businesses and community depend very much on the integrity and round-the-clock availability of technology to function smoothly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would third-party startups and vendors be required to obtain a licence just to offer their services as part of a turnkey solution to organisations?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the proliferation of smart devices, flash drives and devices connected to the Internet, these can all be points of entry for a hacker to cause damage if the user does not have a good basic understanding of digital security.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another possible weak link in the chain is the outsourcing of cybersecurity services to companies that are based overseas.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How does the Ministry intend to ensure the compliance of such companies?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A third possible weak link is the use of third-party vendors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As seen from overseas hacking incidents and data breaches, such as the data breach suffered by Netflix in 2017, poor cybersecurity by third-party vendors has been a consistent problem for years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In 2013, hackers gained access to the network of retail giant Target by first stealing passwords from a third-party vendor dealing with their heating and ventilation systems.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Often, these vendors, also known as network-connected outsiders, are small-sized companies which do not invest much in proper cybersecurity practices, even less so investing in best practices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This has been a problem plaguing many industries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How does the Ministry plan to ensure that such third-party vendors, beyond the 11 identified critical sectors, are also well-regulated?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is, therefore, a need for us to ensure that Singapore has a core talent pool of cybersecurity professionals that can be deployed across the various sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How far are we currently from these target numbers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are the plans to ensure that we have a strong sustained pipeline of local talents to service this growing industry?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Harnessing the enthusiasm of the “white hat” hacker community is a step in the right direction and I would like to propose for the Ministry to consider grooming a local community of “white hat” hackers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, clear boundaries and protocols would need to be drawn and the Ministry would need to think about how to best support and manage the group.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the extent, speed, increasing sophistication and trend of high-profile cyberattacks, this Bill is timely.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are seeing an increasing trend of ransomware.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Ransomware, like Wannacry, that everyone has cited, as well as Samsam, have targeted high profiles like multinational corporations (MNCs), critical infrastructure providers, even hospitals and education institutions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This shows us the extent of disruption that ransomware can inflict.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Malware affects files, computers and mobile devices by encrypting and locking data, rendering them inaccessible and, in most cases, leading to a loss of data and impacting operations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Once inside the network, it gives control of the management inside the network.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As more businesses digitalise and technology progressively influences the way we live, work and play, such attacks will have wide-reaching impact.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the physical world, customers place their trust in businesses to provide quality services and to handle their information appropriately.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To meet these requirements for cybersecurity, one constraint that we all must recognise is that of the availability of skills and knowledgeable cybersecurity specialists.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There has been a lot of discussion on costs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The reason for that high cost that everyone is envisaging is because of this lack of skills or the need to build this base of deep skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the growing demand for cybersecurity skills, building this talent base, we all have to recognise, will take time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clause 5(l) of the Bill outlines the duties and functions of the Commissioner to promote, develop, maintain and improve competencies and professional standards of persons working in the field of cybersecurity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister share the plans to build this talent base and what is being done to ensure that we have sufficient cybersecurity skills and capabilities in Singapore to meet the current and, more importantly, future demands?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill also recognises that for cybersecurity to be effective, it must start at the top, with owners or leaders of CIIs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Building cybersecurity awareness and culture across an organisation requires a strong tone from the top.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, it is interesting to see Part 3 of the Bill clearly outlining the accountability of owners of CIIs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This sends a strong message that leaders own and are accountable for cybersecurity in the organisation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will keep cybersecurity top of mind in the organisation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Building resilience is at the core and spirit of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To achieve cybersecurity, we must not only ensure compliance but, more importantly, an understanding of a mindset change of all stakeholders of Singapore’s CIIs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While measures are put in place for compliance, people are one of our weakest links.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Employees must understand the impact of their actions on cybersecurity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the increasing sophistication and social engineering, targeted phishing emails are not as easily detected.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is becoming more difficult to tell a malicious email from a legitimate email.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, cybersecurity awareness and keeping cybersecurity top of mind are key.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Apart from cybersecurity professionals, training and building resilience of all employees and users of CII is as essential.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is not a trivial task, and organisations will need support to achieve this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister share what will be done to support organisations in this aspect?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must also recognise that it is not a matter of “if” but “when” there will be a breach.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Organisations must have processes and tools to detect cyber threats or incidences.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Most importantly, organisations must have in place processes to take action to recover and minimise the potential impact of the breach.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As Singapore strives to be a Smart Nation, cybersecurity is critical.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Ensuring cybersecurity and resilience of our CII will require a strong partnership amongst stakeholders in the ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To effectively fight cyber threats, organisations and the Government must work together as no one has all the knowledge or resources to do it alone.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For a start, there must be two-way information sharing and feedback.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: By sharing plans on how data collected or submitted to the Commissioner will be used and how it will be used, will enable owners of CIIs to better understand how the data they submit are used.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will help build trust amongst stakeholders to share and, more importantly, work together to combat cyber threats.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With our dependence on the digital world, we can only expect the exposure to cyber threats to increase.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is crucial that our Smart Nation aspirations must go hand in hand with resilient cybersecurity systems.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This makes the Cybersecurity Bill an essential move forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Certainly, investments in cybersecurity could lead to rising business costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For small and medium enterprises (SMEs) already struggling to stay afloat, this will create additional financial stress.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With more cross-company collaboration and outsourcing occurring these days, it is crucial that this becomes a nationwide effort.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would be just like how suppliers for the banking industry would have to adhere to the Banking Secrecy Act.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Data sharing and exchange will be compromised if even just one organisation is careless with their approach on data security.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Resultantly, some companies may then pass down the cost of cybersecurity measures to the consumers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Cybersecurity is often likened to insurance and similarly scorned for the same reasons.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Its necessity is often overlooked until a crisis happens.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would be largely attributed to loss of reputation and potential business, remedial measures, as well as lawsuits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, having a sound cybersecurity system in place would be more cost-effective in the long run.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, as cybersecurity is still unfamiliar territory, some companies may under-invest or over-invest in the wrong systems.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This could mean plenty of administrative work back and forth, when the time, effort and other resources may be better spent on constantly shoring up cybersecurity defences instead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At this point, only penetration testing and managed security operations centre (SOC) monitoring service providers will require licensing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the gig economy blooming, there will be no doubt cybersecurity professionals who provide their services as freelancers will increase.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Cybersecurity professionals deal with sensitive information in large quantities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, is there a need for this to be better regulated?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is it not vital to ensure that they are adequately skilled and possess the right disposition to provide services of such a delicate nature?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the topic of handling sensitive information, some hold reservations that the authorities, while conducting their investigations, would intrude on personal privacy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there safeguards in place for the broad investigation powers to ensure that there is no misuse of authority, whether unintentional or not?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the public be assured that their information is in safe hands?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Meanwhile, we also have the Computer Misuse Act (CMA), formerly the CMCA, as well as existing pieces of legislation, like the Banking Secrecy Act, which also address cybersecurity and data protection issues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there overlapping policies, and how would the new Bill interact with and complement the existing pieces of legislation that we have now?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Enhancing our cybersecurity defences is the next logical move in the face of an increasingly digitalised society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, in May 2017, billionaire businessman Warren Buffett said to his investors that cybersecurity could be the number one problem for mankind.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must put in place laws to safeguard our critical cyber systems and infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have three points of concern, namely, on costs, processes and manpower needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In meeting the requirements, CII sectors will have to impose more stringent requirements on their systems or require their vendors to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will inevitably lead to higher costs, as pointed out by Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, it will work with the sectors to streamline requirements so that they can minimise compliance costs incurred because of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For sectors that face greater complications in meeting the requirements, are there existing schemes that they can tap on for this purpose?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What is the timeline for the implementation of these compliance measures?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Companies might not only need time to ramp up their compliance capabilities but also need technical guidance from MCI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we must not compromise on security, we must ensure that the reporting processes are not unnecessarily onerous.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Companies and their staff already face substantial reporting requirements to other Government bodies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must seek to rationalise compliance for ease of operations without compromising on security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While a strong CSA is necessary for our cybersecurity, it must not also intrude upon privacy unnecessarily.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Ministry has assured that there are safeguards in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And it will adopt a calibrated approach, depending on the severity of attacks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry also share more if it will adopt a tiered or classification system that would spell out the scope or limits of investigation, depending on the level of severity of the incident or attacks?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the security agencies have used threat-level systems to decide on the intensity of preparation and fortification that needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could a similar system be put in place so that stakeholders and parties involved will have a clearer picture of what is required of them should a cyberattack or breach of systems happen?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And more importantly, the requirements needed of them during peacetime as it affects business costs and manpower requirements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While our IHLs have been training more students and the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) has introduced Professional Conversion Programmes (PCPs) for the IT sector, and they have been in place for some time now, would the supply be sufficient?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry work with the Ministry of Education (MOE), MOM and even the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) to ensure that there will be sufficient manpower to meet our future needs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the attacks may originate somewhere, being a technology hub in Southeast Asia means that we have a high amount of Internet traffic from other countries going through us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are a hub with high inter-trade and data connectivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is inevitable that some attacks will originate from Singapore and other similar hubs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, it is also our global responsibility to stop attacks where possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is also an opportunity to provide a trusted gateway for countries and businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It establishes Singapore as a secure business node.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must not stop at exploring and developing ways for us to be used as a gateway for global cybersecurity.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With our Smart Nation initiative and Government-wide move towards digital transformation of our processes, procedures and data management approaches, cybersecurity inadvertently becomes a concern that needs immediate address.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While a lot are in this Cybersecurity Bill, there are, however, several concerns that I have in the implementation of this Bill that is to be enacted.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are their track records studied, and are the employees all screened?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How sure can the Government be in ensuring security and privacy of matters pertaining to the Government, with these third-party cybersecurity service providers and licensees having access to such privileged information?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, we know that cyber hackers and attackers are always, at least, two steps ahead.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I appreciate the focus of the Bill to put in place a penetration testing service to search for vulnerabilities and compromises in the computing system of our public sector and Civil Service outfits, how do we stay ahead of the curve and stay relevant and secure?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do cybersecurity service providers and licensees ensure that the personnel who are helping them to search for these vulnerabilities and compromises are up to speed with what potential cyber hackers or attackers are or will be doing?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sustained efforts to ensure awareness in cybersecurity training of our public and Civil Service officers, so that they are able to recognise potential and actual cybersecurity threats, need to be carried out as well.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, this approach has to be nationwide, even to users of public services, such as students and the general public.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Public education to increase awareness and identification of potential and actual cybersecurity threats must also be done to support the provisions of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Public and Civil Service officers, as well as students in our public education institutions, need to understand and recognise when certain emails, hyperlinks or even mobile applications could risk the integrity and compromise the safety of connected computing systems in our various public offices, institutions or schools.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our cybersecurity public awareness programmes must continue and be further enhanced.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, to what extent is data shared among our public sector officers currently in designing and implementing better policies or programmes for the public?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And with this new cybersecurity legislation, how will that sharing of data and information be impacted?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Everything from our transport system and fire departments to our hospitals and military relies on the availability of sustained access to computer systems and networks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This also means that a successful cyberattack on our CII would not simply pose a threat to our way of life but could seriously endanger our national security.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I applaud MCI and CSA's efforts to develop the resilience needed to ensure that when we are attacked, we will stay strong.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen how technology, used in the right way, has uplifted people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ride-sharing and food delivery applications have given many people a new outlet for income, and entrepreneurs have embraced e-commerce to expand their market.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Technology has helped many to climb the socio-economic ladder.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ensuring our CIIs are resilient to a large-scale cyberattack is important.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But there is more to who we are as a country than just 11 critical sectors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Small businesses must be resilient to hacks and learn how to maintain business operations, but regular Singaporeans should also be armed with tools to stay safe online.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, how can we help our SMEs, our Instagram influencers and first-time e-retailers stay safe and be able to continue their business operations when they are hacked?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How can we help the older generation, the aunties and uncles, to learn the best practices of using the Internet so that they can avoid becoming victims of cybercrimes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The risks that regular people face online are increasing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As many have mentioned, last year, thousands were affected when WannaCry ransomware hit our shores.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the threat can come from within Singapore, too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The very fact that we are a connected and smart country means that we are more at risk to cyberattacks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An idea to start with is with our young ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The UK, for example, has set aside £20 million to fund co-curricular activity (CCA) clubs in schools that focus on cybersecurity training.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This not only teaches children how to be good online citizens, but it also creates a pipeline of future cybersecurity specialists.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would MCI and CSA consider working with the Ministry of Education (MOE) on this?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another possibility would be to provide grants to SMEs to beef up their cybersecurity awareness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many businessmen may be unaware that being hacked could ruin their company.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Smaller companies do not have large IT footprints but will face serious operational risks if their systems were down.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Precision engineering firms would not be able to continue to manufacture if they were attacked by ransomware.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Others would lose customers if customer data was to be hacked.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would MCI and CSA work with SPRING Singapore or the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) to help SMEs and startups pay for anti-virus software or hire consultants for cybersecurity reviews?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, we can explore ways to do more for our most vulnerable residents – the older generation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have residents who are 90-year-old grandparents who check their email and WhatsApp constantly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To them, technology is no longer just a novelty, but an integral part of daily life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, these residents are the most vulnerable to hacking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would CSA work with the People's Association (PA) to develop programmes to teach the fundamentals of cybersecurity?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would give CSA greater visibility on the types of hacks that are happening in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, every day that a breach goes unreported is another day that people are at risk of identity theft or credit theft.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Anything we can do to improve our national resilience to outside threats is a positive step.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But let us not forget that thousands of SMEs and millions of Singaporeans still do not know how to stay safe in cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We will never be truly resilient unless all of us, collectively as Singaporeans, can effectively mitigate the risks of being online.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: According to the Check Point report, Singapore was likely used as a gateway for attacks based elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In recent years, we have also witnessed a surge in spates of cyber incidents on a global scale, some of which have hit home.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As Singapore develops into a highly-interconnected Smart Nation, we will become an increasingly attractive target for cybercriminals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As more aspects of our lives go digital, fallout from such attacks will become even more extensive and breakdowns in provision of essential services could result in loss of property, sensitive data and even lives not only on a national scale but on a global scale.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is, therefore, timely that we put in place robust regulatory infrastructure to govern cybersecurity matters in Singapore and maintain high cybersecurity standards to protect critical systems and data.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While I am supportive of the Bill, I do have some questions and suggestions which I would like to raise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I classify them into what I call the 5Cs: (a) Classification, (b) Compliance Costs, (c) Compromises and Concerns, (d) Continuing Education and (e) Contingency Planning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Having such a mechanism would allow organisations to definitively determine if they are a CII so that they can better plan for their operational costs and resource requirements in order to comply with the requirements of CIIs under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By the same token, are there any measures in place to ensure that the cost of compliance as CIIs do not trickle down extensively to the consumer?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, CSA is given broad investigative powers under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These powers should be exercised with care to ensure that innovation is not curtailed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As part of its educational outreach in the NTUC's U Associate’s network, The Internet Society, Singapore Chapter (ISOC.SG) collected feedback from stakeholders on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: ISOC.SG found that the general thrust of the Bill was widely accepted although there was concern that overly broad investigative powers would curtail innovation and the technology industry.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A balance, without compromising cybersecurity, must be found.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: An example is allowing investigation and removal of anything, servers and data included, at any time.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Although powers are used to combat security threats, too much data could be taken or disruptive actions could result if powers are poorly exercised.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With possible implications on our status/efforts to become a data hub, the reasonable use of powers, perhaps with a chance to challenge a decision, makes sense.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As a general point, overly broad powers usually affect innovation because of fear and less risk-taking.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, with this Bill and our Industry Transformation efforts across several sectors, I look forward to more job opportunities for those with cybersecurity skills.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This will avail new entrants as well as those already within the profession to upgrade and keep abreast with the latest developments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Although there were reservations by practitioners during the public consultation to license practitioners in this field, I submit that it is still good to align and benchmark the skills and competencies of cybersecurity professionals locally and with global accreditations and provide more platforms for continuing education and professional development to ensure they stay relevant and current within the practice of cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To this end, the Labour Movement hopes to partner the various associations in this sector and the cybersecurity professionals in this journey to provide continuous learning, growth and career progression opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: NTUC and ISOC.SG are supportive of continuing efforts, as every Singaporean is online to some degree and a stakeholder in the security of the Internet, to avail users to tools and resources and building cybersecurity awareness to help enhance cybersecurity and build trust online.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By inculcating that cybersecurity DNA or genetic code into all Singaporeans, we will also create a world-class future-ready workforce that can differentiate itself to employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the recent Petya ransomware attack in mid-2017, a number of companies under the global marketing services group WPP were affected by Petya.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Singapore employees of a company under WPP were reported to be scrambling to follow instructions on how to deal with Petya after the attack.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They were told to log off from the office wi-fi network or servers, and made arrangements to work remotely.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some worked from home using their personal computers, while other teams met in public spaces, such as cafes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Are our enterprises equipped to take steps to prevent cyber incidents from occurring?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Are there response and business continuity plans in place which they can implement if they are subject to a cyberattack?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To raise our people’s awareness of cybersecurity, will there be a pervasive rollout of cybersecurity messaging and e-learning to individuals so that they are equipped with the requisite knowledge and skills to prevent cyber incidents and know what to do when faced with one, as has been done for SG Secure?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Are there plans to develop cybersecurity tools that all individuals can use to safeguard their devices against cyberattacks?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There could be publicly available online quizzes to understand cybersecurity and prevention tips.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These tools could perhaps be developed by trainees undergoing training to be cybersecurity professionals who are placed with cybersecurity enterprises or startups in the business of developing these tools.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We can even provide free-to-use anti-virus software available for all households to utilise, especially since we are moving towards a Smart Nation and we are all so virtually connected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   I support this Bill but I would like to raise three points here.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am also concerned that the cost will be passed on to the consumers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Therefore, I urge the Government, companies and our citizens to stay alert and be prepared.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In English): With that, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the pivotal role that CII owners play, I would like to understand how the essential services and CIIs are identified, together with their owners.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In instances where business operations are international and computer systems are housed outside Singapore, how would CII owners be identified and held accountable for their cybersecurity responsibilities?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is heartening to note that MCI and CSA have been forthcoming and open to suggestions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Bill would likely bring about increased compliance costs as well as organisational change to businesses.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would there be adequate time given to them for them to comply?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And when there are cyberattacks, how do we balance the need for incident reporting and investigation requirements when CIIs may be putting efforts simultaneously to restore services targeted by cyberattacks?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Standards or codes of practice issued or approved under the Bill should be aligned with globally compatible policies and benchmarks to help CII owners as much as possible.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given rapid developments globally to tackle cyber threats, how would the Bill take into account global developments and evolving standards?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Bill is bold as it covers both the public and private sectors, recognising that cybercriminals do not distinguish between such boundaries.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, concerns about the extent of powers a proposed Cybersecurity Bill would give the Government has emerged, underscoring the ever-present tension between security and protection of privacy.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, various laws prevent the disclosure of personal information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Banks, for example, owe their customers a duty of confidentiality under the Banking Act.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Similarly, organisations cannot use or disclose personal data without individuals’ consent under the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is there scope then for the Bill to better address the intent of the Bill with existing prohibitions on disclosure?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They offer many new and exciting opportunities but, at the same time, present several challenges, including increasing our vulnerability to cyberattacks.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Cybersecurity Bill would help fortify our systems against cyberattacks and, notwithstanding my clarifications, is definitely a step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   Cybersecurity cannot be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Cyberattacks are becoming more sophisticated and can cripple our CII.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This can have serious repercussions for our nation’s ability to function and deliver essential services to our citizens.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Bill sets out the responsibilities of CII owners.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: CII owners have to be identified correctly and their responsibilities accordingly scoped so that they face the right impetus to invest in cybersecurity for the sake of the nation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There will be conflict between the need to uphold cybersecurity and the need to protect the privacy of information, but we should not shy away from exploring where the boundaries are and find the right balance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): With that, I support the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Some Members, Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Mr Pritam Singh and Ms Sun Xueling, asked how the Bill will apply to systems that are providing essential services but located overseas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Overall, a significant majority of such systems are based wholly or partly in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Owners of CII that are partly located in Singapore will still have to comply with their obligations under the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Given Singapore’s interconnectivity, it is inevitable that some computer systems serving important functions in Singapore are connected globally and may also be located wholly outside Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These computer systems could also be operated by international organisations based abroad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There may also be potential conflicts with other countries’ regulatory regimes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To facilitate investigations of cybersecurity threats and incidents that may originate overseas, the Government has made significant efforts to develop strong international partnerships and linkages with overseas Computer Emergency Response Teams (CERTs).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CSA will work closely with its foreign counterparts for such investigations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ms Joan Peirera and Mr Melvin Yong asked if the cybersecurity of CII would be affected if their owners choose not to impose requirements on their vendors or if such vendors were not regulated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CSA will work with the sector regulators and CII owners to define the boundaries of the systems that will be designated as CII, on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Many engage third-party vendors to support their CII.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In deciding which vendors to engage and what conditions to impose on their vendors, CII owners should carry out the necessary risk assessments and due diligence to ensure that their obligations under the Bill are complied with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CII owners will be required under the Bill to conduct regular cybersecurity audits to ensure that their obligations are met.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This provides an added layer of assurance that the CII would be in compliance with cybersecurity codes of practice and standards of performance, as required under the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ms Thanaletchimi suggested establishing an accredited framework for a national cybersecurity audit for CII stakeholders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There are already multiple layers of IT audit regimes established within the 11 sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We are mindful that another layer of national cybersecurity audit could potentially result in CII stakeholders experiencing audit fatigue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For now, CSA plans to tap on existing sector audit regimes to ensure that the security measures are effective in protecting the CIIs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To ensure an acceptable standard of practice, CSA will provide audit guidance to auditors and track the audit outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Darryl David asked how CII and essential services are determined, while Assoc Prof Daniel Goh suggested that higher education and research institutions be considered essential services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In arriving at the list of essential services in the First Schedule, we took reference from section 15A of CMCA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We also studied the definition of "essential services" in other jurisdictions before identifying a total of 11 sectors in Singapore delivering essential services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These sectors provide services that are essential to the national security, defence, foreign relations, economy, public health, public safety or public order of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For each sector, CSA worked closely with the relevant sector regulator to identify the essential services within the sector, as well as the computers and computer systems that would be CII.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Higher education and research institutions are not considered essential services at this point in time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Nonetheless, we do not preclude that new essential services may arise in the future, and the Minister may amend the list of essential services in the First Schedule if necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked if there is a mechanism in place whereby organisations can check with CSA on whether they are CII owners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There is no need for organisations to make self-assessments as to whether their computer or computer systems fulfil the criteria of a CII.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Prior to designating a computer or computer system as a CII, CSA will consult its owner and the relevant sector regulator to identify whether it is responsible for the provision of any of the essential services listed in the First Schedule.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Organisations whose computers or computer systems are designated as CII will be notified in writing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CII owners will be given an opportunity to submit representations to the Commissioner if they disagree with the Commissioner's decision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: They may also appeal to the Minister against the designation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: However, the Minister's decision on an appeal will be final.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: MCI and CSA have already consulted with the sector regulators in identifying potential CIIs and engaged the potential CII owners twice since July 2016.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Hence, potential CII owners would already know who they are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The process for identifying and designating new CII in the future will be similarly considered and be consultative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Some Members – Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Sun Xueling – asked whether the incident reporting and investigation requirements under the Bill could be too onerous for CII owners, especially when they are potential victims of cyberattacks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Given the importance of CII to Singapore, it is necessary to provide for their proactive protection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, clause 14 requires CII owners to establish mechanisms and processes to detect cybersecurity threats and incidents in respect of the CII.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CII owners are also required to promptly report to CSA cybersecurity incidents in relation to their CII and any computer or computer systems connected with the CII that are under their control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This will enable CSA to have better oversight of incidents happening across sectors, and to take the necessary actions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There is no obligation for a CII owner to report a cybersecurity incident in respect of other infrastructure that it owns, where such infrastructure is not connected to the CII.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Under clauses 19 and 20, CII owners are required to cooperate with CSA during the investigation of cybersecurity threats and incidents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I will elaborate on CSA's exercise of investigation powers later in my speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about the incident reporting threshold for CII owners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: All CII owners, regardless of whether they are local or foreign companies, will need to report to CSA cybersecurity incidents that occur on or that affect their CII.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: A cybersecurity incident on a CII is defined as an act or activity carried out without lawful authority on or through the CII that jeopardises or adversely affects its cybersecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As Mr Pritam Singh pointed out, details of what constitutes a prescribed incident and the form and manner of reporting will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: When exercising these powers, the Commissioner will be mindful that the owners of the computer systems in question are typically also victims.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CSA will be providing further details to guide CII owners in incident reporting, such as relevant forms and guidelines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: On the other hand, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Mr Louis Ng called for mandatory reporting of all cybersecurity incidents to CSA for more holistic protection of Singapore's cyberspace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Making the reporting of cybersecurity incidents a requirement under the Bill will be both resource-intensive for CSA as well as companies in Singapore, especially our SMEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Today, all companies, including owners of computer systems that are not CII, can already voluntarily report cybersecurity incidents to CSA through the Singapore Cyber Emergency Response Team (SingCERT).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: On top of this, the Bill will provide CSA with powers to investigate cybersecurity threats and incidents pertaining to computer systems in Singapore, including computer systems that are not CII.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Patrick Tay asked whether there are programmes to help CII owners comply with their obligations under the Bill, while Ms Thanaletchimi suggested that staff of organisations that own CII attend cybersecurity awareness programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: On the other hand, Ms Sun Xueling and Mr Desmond Choo asked about the time that CII owners will be given to implement cybersecurity measures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CLIPS will focus on establishing clarity on the roles and responsibilities between the sector regulators and the CII owners and identifying and resolving any operational issues pertaining to the respective sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, these include harmonising policies and streamlining audits and incident reporting processes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The need to step up protection of CII is urgent but, where necessary, CSA will also give CII owners sufficient time to undertake preparations and planning, prior to issuing the cybersecurity codes of practice or standards of performance for each sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Assistant Commissioners, also known as ACs, are senior officers appointed from the 11 CII sectors and will be able to advise the Commissioner on the necessary requirements, taking into consideration the unique contexts and complexities of their respective sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad provided many useful suggestions to help CII owners meet their obligations under the Bill, including sharing best practices and benchmarks, and providing support for their R&D efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He also asked if the cybersecurity readiness of the CII owners will be benchmarked.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Today, CSA assesses the cybersecurity readiness of the CII sectors and shares this information with CII owners to help them improve the cybersecurity of their CII.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will consider Mr Zaqy Mohamad's other suggestions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: And I agree with Ms Thanaletchimi that we need to establish mechanisms to inform organisations if they are potential targets, and advise them on precautionary measures that they could take.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CSA currently shares information on cybersecurity threats and vulnerabilities with the CII sectors so that appropriate actions can be taken promptly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The CERTs overseeing specific sectors also issue advisories to the operators in their respective sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Several Members – Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Ms Sun Xueling and Mr Desmond Choo – asked about the costs that CII owners and other businesses may have to incur in implementing cybersecurity measures, while Mr Patrick Tay asked whether there are any measures to ensure that compliance costs do not trickle down to consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Cybersecurity is a collective responsibility, and we must all do our part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Today, many CII owners have already put in place cybersecurity measures arising from regulations in sectors, such as banking and finance and infocomm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Bill aims to strengthen the cybersecurity of CII in all sectors, including those that currently do not have any cybersecurity requirements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The requirements under the Bill have been carefully scoped and are considered not too onerous.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There will be cost implications for some CII owners who will have to strengthen the cybersecurity posture of their computer systems to meet the requirements of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To minimise regulatory costs, we will work with sector regulators to streamline the cybersecurity audit and incident reporting processes in order to harmonise cybersecurity requirements under the Bill and in their respective sectors, wherever possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It is also in the interest of CII owners and their vendors to spend adequately on cybersecurity measures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: They should consider not only the upfront cost of such measures, but also the cost of potential breaches, including the intangible costs arising from any damage to their reputation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: If organisations follow security-by-design practices, they will spend less overall in the long run to fix cybersecurity issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ms Sun Xueling and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how the Cybersecurity Bill is intended to interact with existing legislation that have cybersecurity or data protection requirements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Darryl David asked how the Bill will be administered in view of existing agencies with cybersecurity roles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, in the event of a cybersecurity incident, the Telecommunications Act will continue to govern licensees under that Act for resulting telecommunications service disruptions, while the PDPA will continue to govern companies and individuals in the area of personal data breaches.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As mentioned earlier, there are already some laws and regulations in Singapore that deal with various aspects of cybersecurity, such as in the banking and finance, and infocomm sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In certain cases, such sectoral requirements may be more stringent or wider in scope than those in the Cybersecurity Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The AC from the sector will play a key role in ensuring that CII owners do not face conflicting requirements under the Cybersecurity Bill and in sectoral regulations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This will help minimise the regulatory burden on CII owners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I wish to clarify that we are not establishing a new agency under the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Chief Executive of CSA will be appointed as the Commissioner, and he will be supported by CSA staff and the ACs who are intended to be senior officers from the sector regulators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In many instances, the CII owners will interact with the ACs appointed from their sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about the relationship between the Cybersecurity Bill and CMA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Darryl David asked how the Government would deal with individuals who hack into a website to spread falsehoods, while Mr Henry Kwek asked for a re-examination of the penalties for misuse of access to data, especially if the perpetrators are cybersecurity professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Cybersecurity Bill and CMA are complementary, given that cybersecurity and cybercrimes are closely related.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Cybersecurity Bill provides for investigation powers in clauses 19 and 20.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These investigation powers apply only to the assessment of the impact of cybersecurity threats and incidents, and to the prevention of further harm and further incidents from arising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The investigation of cybercrimes and the prosecution of their perpetrators are different issues covered by CMA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Hence, it is important that the Cybersecurity Bill and CMA are kept separate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This will also make them less vulnerable to cybercrime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The unauthorised use of or modification of computer material and the unauthorised use of computer service are cybercrimes which are offences under CMA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CMA is under the purview of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and the Police.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Depending on the facts of the case, cybersecurity professionals who misuse their access to data may be prosecuted under CMA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CSA, with the investigation powers under the Cybersecurity Bill, will work with MHA and the Police to better protect computer systems in Singapore, especially CII, against cybersecurity incidents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: However, neither CMA nor this Bill is intended to address the threat of fake news.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Several Members − Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Desmond Choo, Ms Sun Xueling, Mr Darryl David, Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Saktiandi Supaat − asked about the broad investigation powers provided to the Commissioner by the Bill, including whether such powers would curtail innovation or intrude into personal privacy and how such powers would be used judiciously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: How an incident will be classified depends on the facts of the case at hand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To be clear, all organisations, regardless of whether they are local or foreign, are required to cooperate with CSA during the investigation of cybersecurity threats and incidents pertaining to computers or computer systems in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We recognise the need to balance operational expediency with the proportionate and judicious exercise of power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Investigation officers cannot investigate and remove equipment "at any time".

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, the Commissioner’s authorisation is required before cybersecurity officers and authorised officers can exercise more intrusive investigation powers under clause 20.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There will be a governance process within CSA to ensure that the investigation powers are exercised responsibly and in accordance with the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CSA will also consider providing guidelines to the public, to advise the owners of computer systems on what they should do during investigations of cybersecurity threats or incidents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Commissioner will determine the appropriate measures to take during investigations of cybersecurity threats and incidents, in consultation with the owner of the computer or computer system whenever possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To address Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan's point, this will be the case, regardless of the type of computer system or technology involved, including cloud services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, the Commissioner may take possession of any computer or equipment to carry out further examination or analysis with the consent of the owner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: However, if there is no consent from the owner, clause 20(5) clearly sets out the conditions that must be met before the Commissioner can authorise the exercise of this power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Prior to deploying more intrusive investigation tools, such as network-scanning software, which are necessary when responding to cybersecurity incidents, CSA will, wherever possible, notify the computer system owners and follow appropriate protocols.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The measures and requirements are mainly technical, operational and procedural in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, CII owners may be required to implement network perimeter defence devices, such as firewalls, or to perform regular vulnerability scanning of their systems, to identify potential loopholes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These measures are non-intrusive with respect to personal privacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, to aid in the detection of cybersecurity threats, information, such as network logs, indicators of compromise as well as systems event and audit logs, may be requested.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Furthermore, the Commissioner’s requests for information from CII owners are carefully scoped for specific purposes, such as information pertaining to the technical design and configuration of a CII.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Commissioner does not have direct or continuous access to the data of any CII owner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As mentioned in my opening speech, the Bill protects information disclosed to CSA under the Bill by requiring persons who obtain it in the course of performing their functions or discharging their duties under the Bill to keep it confidential, and by specifying the circumstances under which it can be disclosed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: With the exception of clause 23, the Bill does not require persons to disclose any information that is prohibited by any other law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Minister is constrained by the language of clause 23 when exercising his powers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked whether the Bill would cover less mainstream cybersecurity services, such as white hat or ethical hackers, while Mr Melvin Yong asked if the Ministry could consider encouraging a local community of white hats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
